pos: n. (the Castilian university city whose theological school argued the rights of the American Indians and whose Hebraist Luis de Leon was imprisoned by the Inquisition)
etymology: From Latin Salmantica, a Vettones town on the Tormes, of pre-Roman origin.
biblical_def: Salamanca held the oldest university in Spain, chartered in 1218, and in the sixteenth century the most important faculty of theology in Catholic Europe. Francisco de Vitoria, holding the prime chair from 1526, delivered the lectures on the Indies which argued that the American peoples were true owners of their lands, that neither papal grant nor imperial title conferred a right of conquest, that unbelief forfeits no property, and that a war of conquest for religion is unjust; from that root grew the modern law of nations. Domingo de Soto, Melchor Cano and later Francisco Suarez continued the school. Salamanca also tried its own: Luis de Leon, Augustinian and Hebraist, was imprisoned by the Inquisition from 1572 to 1576 for preferring the Hebrew text to the Vulgate and for translating the Song of Songs into Spanish, and resumed his chair with the remark that he had been saying when interrupted. The dictionary records Salamanca as proof that conscience survived in the Spanish church, and that it was punished there.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a chair as a professorship; conquest as the subjection of a country by force; dominion as the right of possession and use; Hebraist is not in Webster, but Hebrew is the language of the Hebrews; and conscience as the internal judge of right and wrong.
webster_full: CHAIR, n. A seat of justice or of authority; a professorship in a university or college.
CONQUEST, n. The act of conquering; the subjection of a country or people by war or force; that which is conquered.
DOMINION, n. Sovereign authority; the power of governing; the territory under a government; right of possession and use.
HEBREW, n. A Jew; one of the descendants of Abraham; the language of the Hebrews.
CONSCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge, or judgment of right and wrong; the faculty which decides on the lawfulness of our own actions.
scriptures: Pro 31:9
Open thy mouth, judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy.
Rob not the poor, because he is poor: neither oppress the afflicted in the gate:
Isa 1:17
Learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow.
Mic 6:8
He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
corruption_summary: Castilian university city of Vitoria's lectures on the rights of the American Indians and of Luis de Leon's imprisonment for preferring the Hebrew text.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the theology of conquest, and the honour belongs here to the men who refused it from inside the conquering church. Vitoria taught at the height of Spanish power that heathen nations own their land, that the pope cannot grant what is not his, and that no war for the faith is just. He was not a Protestant and he was not disciplined; he was simply right, and he reasoned from the law that protects the weak against the strong: “Rob not the poor, because he is poor: neither oppress the afflicted in the gate” (Pro 22:22).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is that the defence of the defenceless is an office and not a sentiment. Solomon gives it to the king as a duty of speech, “Open thy mouth, judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy” (Pro 31:9), and Isaiah lists the acts that constitute a reformed nation: “relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow” (Isa 1:17). The whole requirement is three clauses long, “to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God” (Mic 6:8), and the dictionary observes that the same university which produced that teaching also imprisoned a man for reading Hebrew. A faculty may be braver about distant injustice than about the tribunal down the street.

pos: n. (the old Castilian capital where the Laws of Burgos of 1512 first attempted to regulate Spanish treatment of the American Indians)
etymology: From Spanish burgo, a fortified town, from Germanic burg, a stronghold.
biblical_def: Burgos was the capital of old Castile, the seat of its counts and of a great cathedral begun in 1221, and the city of Rodrigo Diaz, the Cid. Its claim here is legislative. After the Dominican Antonio de Montesinos preached at Santo Domingo in 1511 denouncing the enslavement of the Taino, the crown convened theologians and jurists, and the Laws of Burgos of 1512 were the result: the first European legislation on the treatment of a colonised people, limiting labour, requiring instruction in the faith, forbidding the beating of Indians and the taking of children, and regulating the encomienda rather than abolishing it. They were widely ignored, and were superseded by the New Laws of 1542 after Las Casas. The dictionary records Burgos as the first point at which a European power admitted in law that its colonial subjects had rights, and admits plainly that the admission was made small, enforced feebly, and made at all only because a friar preached a sermon that cost him his career.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines slavery as the state of entire subjection to another; labour as exertion of body or mind; a law as a rule of action prescribed by authority; oppression as the act of burdening unreasonably; and restitution as the act of returning what was taken.
webster_full: SLAVERY, n. The state of entire subjection of one person to the will of another; bondage.
LABOR, n. Exertion of muscular strength, or bodily exertion which occasions weariness; toil; work.
LAW, n. A rule, particularly an established or permanent rule, prescribed by the supreme power of a state to its subjects.
OPPRESSION, n. The act of oppressing; cruelty; severity; the imposition of unreasonable burdens, either in imposing labor or taxes.
RESTITUTION, n. The act of returning or restoring to a person some thing or right that he has been unjustly deprived of.
scriptures: And he that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death.
Thou shalt not oppress an hired servant that is poor and needy, whether he be of thy brethren, or of thy strangers that are in thy land within thy gates:
Jas 5:4

Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth.
Isa 58:6
Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke?
corruption_summary: Old Castilian capital where the Laws of Burgos of 1512 first regulated Spanish treatment of the American Indians, after Montesinos's sermon of 1511.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is forced labour conducted by Christians on baptised people with a licence from the crown, and the dictionary refuses the usual defence that nobody then knew better. Montesinos knew in 1511 and said so in a pulpit; the theologians at Burgos knew enough to legislate; and the law they wrote regulated the system instead of ending it. The statute Moses gave on the subject is not a regulation but a capital prohibition: “he that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death” (Exo 21:16).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. The law protects the labourer by name, whether he is a brother or a stranger, “Thou shalt not oppress an hired servant that is poor and needy” (Deu 24:14), and James says what becomes of withheld wages, that they cry out and are heard: “the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth” (Jas 5:4). Isaiah defines the fast God chooses as an act of release and not a feeling, “to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free” (Isa 58:6). Burgos adjusted the burden. The text says to take it off.

pos: n. (the Castilian city and see whose converso community was formed by the conversions of 1411 and broken by the tribunal in 1485)
etymology: From Latin Segovia, a Celtiberian town name, from a root meaning victory or strength.
biblical_def: Segovia stands on a rock above the Castilian plateau beneath its Roman aqueduct, a wool city, a royal residence, and the place where Isabella was proclaimed queen in 1474. Its church history is the history of its Jewish quarter. The preaching of Vincent Ferrer and the legislation that followed from 1411 produced mass conversions here as elsewhere in Castile, so that by the middle of the century a large part of the city's merchant and official class were conversos, including men who held office in the cathedral. In 1485 the new tribunal arrived; the synagogue was confiscated, prosecutions followed, and in 1492 the remaining professing Jews were expelled. The dictionary records Segovia as the standard Castilian pattern rather than an exception, and draws from it the conclusion the whole episode forces. Conversions produced by civil pressure create a population that is neither one thing nor the other, and the institution that produced them then persecutes them for the ambiguity it created.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a synagogue as a Jewish congregation or its place of worship; conversion as a change from one faith to another; confiscation as the act of forfeiting to the state; pressure as the act of urging; and sincerity as freedom from hypocrisy.
webster_full: SYNAGOGUE, n. A congregation or assembly of Jews, met for the purpose of worship; the house appropriated to that worship.
CONVERSION, n. In a theological or moral sense, a change of heart or dispositions, in which the enmity of the heart to God is subdued.
CONFISCATION, n. The act of condemning as forfeited, and adjudging to the public treasury.
PRESSURE, n. The act of pressing; urgency; that which afflicts or constrains the mind.
SINCERITY, n. Honesty of mind or intention; freedom from hypocrisy; the quality of being in reality what it appears to be.
scriptures: Rom 10:1
Brethren, my heart's desire and prayer to God for Israel is, that they might be saved.
Rom 9:3
For I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh:
Rom 11:1
I say then, Hath God cast away his people? God forbid. For I also am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin.
For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.
corruption_summary: Castilian city whose large converso class was created by the conversions following 1411 and prosecuted by the tribunal from 1485.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the forced conversion of the Jews, which Spain pursued for a century and which the dictionary names as a sin against the very people to whom the Scriptures were first entrusted. Paul's own posture toward his unbelieving kinsmen is the opposite of a tribunal's, and it is stated as desire and prayer rather than coercion: “my heart's desire and prayer to God for Israel is, that they might be saved” (Rom 10:1). He goes further and wishes himself accursed in their place, “For I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren” (Rom 9:3).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. Paul denies absolutely that God has finished with Israel, asking “Hath God cast away his people? God forbid” (Rom 11:1), which forbids both the contempt that drove the Spanish policy and the triumphalism that often excuses it. And the mechanism of real conversion is interior, which is why a decree cannot produce one: “For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom 10:10). The dictionary holds that the right answer to a synagogue is a preached gospel and a kept promise, and that Segovia offered neither.

pos: n. (the walled Castilian city of Teresa of Avila and of John of Avila, and the see of Priscillian, the first man executed for heresy by a Christian state)
etymology: From Latin Abula, a Vettones town, of pre-Roman origin.
biblical_def: Avila is a small walled city on the Castilian plateau whose intact medieval walls are its emblem, and three names belong to it. Priscillian, bishop of Avila from about 380, taught an ascetic and probably dualist doctrine with a strong emphasis on private study of Scripture and apocryphal books, was condemned by Spanish synods, appealed to the emperor, and was beheaded at Trier in 385 by the usurper Maximus; Ambrose and Martin of Tours both protested the execution. Teresa of Avila, born here in 1515, reformed the Carmelite order into the Discalced observance and wrote the best-known mystical prose in Spanish. Juan de Avila, the apostle of Andalusia, was a preacher and spiritual writer who was himself investigated by the Inquisition. The dictionary records Avila chiefly for Priscillian, because his death in 385 is the hinge at which the church first accepted the execution of a heretic by a Christian magistrate, and Ambrose and Martin were right to protest it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines asceticism is not in Webster, but an ascetic is one who retires for devotion and mortification; mysticism as obscure doctrine; a usurper as one who seizes power unlawfully; execution as the carrying out of a sentence; and excommunication as the ejection from church fellowship.
webster_full: ASCETIC, n. One who retires from the customary business of life and devotes himself to the duties of piety and devotion; a hermit.
MYSTICISM, n. Obscurity of doctrine; the doctrine of the Mystics, who profess a pure, sublime and perfect devotion.
USURPER, n. One who seizes power or possessions without right; one who dispossesses the rightful ruler.
EXECUTION, n. The act of signing and sealing a legal instrument; the carrying into effect a sentence or judgment of court.
EXCOMMUNICATION, n. The act of ejecting from a church; expulsion from the communion of a church and the privileges thereof.
scriptures: (For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)
Tit 3:10
A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject;
But he said, Nay; lest while ye gather up the tares, ye root up also the wheat with them.

Let both grow together until the harvest: and in the time of harvest I will say to the reapers, Gather ye together first the tares, and bind them in bundles to burn them: but gather the wheat into my barn.
corruption_summary: Walled Castilian city of Teresa and John of Avila, and see of Priscillian, beheaded at Trier in 385 as the first man executed for heresy by a Christian state.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the execution of heretics, and 385 is where it begins. The dictionary does not defend Priscillian's doctrine, which the Spanish church had real cause to condemn, and it insists on the distinction the church lost that year: condemnation and exclusion are ecclesiastical acts, and killing is not one of them. Paul's instruction about a divisive man ends at refusal of fellowship: “A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject” (Tit 3:10). The weapons available to the church are named and they are not the sword, since “the weapons of our warfare are not carnal” (2Co 10:4).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is the patience Christ commands in the parable of the tares. The servants propose exactly what Spain would later institutionalise, and are refused: “Nay; lest while ye gather up the tares, ye root up also the wheat with them” (Mat 13:29). The ordered alternative is to wait for a judgment not ours to execute, “Let both grow together until the harvest” (Mat 13:30). Ambrose and Martin of Tours broke communion with the bishops who had procured Priscillian's death, which is the dictionary's model: the right answer to a heretic executed is to condemn both the heresy and the execution.

“Let both grow together until the harvest” (Mat 13:30) — the ordered alternative.

pos: n. (the Asturian capital from which the reconquest began, whose cathedral chamber holds the relics gathered from Toledo in 711)
etymology: From Latin Ovetum, a monastic foundation of 761, of uncertain origin.
biblical_def: Oviedo is the capital of Asturias, the mountain kingdom that survived the Muslim conquest of 711 and from which the reconquest of the peninsula was conducted over the next seven centuries. Alfonso the Second made it his capital about 800 and built the churches of Santa Maria del Naranco and San Miguel de Lillo, the finest surviving pre-Romanesque buildings in Spain. Its cathedral holds the Camara Santa, a chamber built to house relics said to have been carried north out of Toledo ahead of the invading armies, including a cloth claimed as the face-covering of Christ, which drew pilgrims for a thousand years and for a period rivalled Compostela. The dictionary records Oviedo as the point at which a national survival became a religious cult. The Asturian kings genuinely did hold a mountain against an empire, and their descendants attached to that deliverance a chamber of objects, a patron and a legend, which is the ordinary way a people turns a mercy into a possession.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a relic as the remains of a saint preserved for veneration; veneration as the highest degree of respect; a shrine as a case in which sacred things are kept; deliverance as rescue from danger; and a memorial as that which preserves remembrance.
webster_full: RELIC, n. The remains of the body of a saint, or something belonging to a saint, preserved with great respect, as a sacred memorial.
VENERATION, n. The highest degree of respect and reverence; respect mingled with some degree of awe.
SHRINE, n. A case, box or receptacle for depositing sacred things; a sacred place; an altar.
DELIVERANCE, n. Release from captivity, slavery, oppression or any restraint; rescue from danger or any evil.
MEMORIAL, n. That which preserves the memory of something; any thing that serves to keep in memory.
scriptures: He removed the high places, and brake the images, and cut down the groves, and brake in pieces the brasen serpent that Moses had made: for unto those days the children of Israel did burn incense to it: and he called it Nehushtan.
Exo 20:4
Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:
Deu 6:12
Then beware lest thou forget the LORD, which brought thee forth out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage.
Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands.
corruption_summary: Asturian capital from which the reconquest began, whose cathedral chamber holds relics said to have been carried from Toledo in 711.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the veneration of relics, and Oviedo shows the whole mechanism in one chamber: a real deliverance, a set of objects associated with it, and within a few generations a pilgrimage. The dictionary recalls that Scripture records the same process and records its correction. The brazen serpent was a genuine instrument of a genuine mercy, and Hezekiah destroyed it when Israel began to burn incense to it, because “unto those days the children of Israel did burn incense to it” (2Ki 18:4).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. The second commandment governs the matter without reference to the sincerity of the worshipper, “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above” (Exo 20:4), and the psalmist's mockery of idols is precisely a mockery of craftsmanship: “Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands” (Psa 115:4). What a delivered people is commanded instead is memory of the deliverer rather than possession of the tokens: “Then beware lest thou forget the LORD, which brought thee forth out of the land of Egypt” (Deu 6:12). Asturias remembered the chamber and forgot the warning.

pos: n. (the ancient see of Leon whose bishop Symposius was a Priscillianist, and the chief town of the Maragatos)
etymology: From Latin Asturica Augusta, the Augustan city of the Astures.
biblical_def: Astorga was the Roman administrative centre of north-western Spain, called by Pliny a magnificent city, and became one of the oldest sees in the peninsula; its bishops are named in records from the third century. In the Priscillianist crisis of the late fourth and early fifth centuries Astorga was a centre of the party: its bishop Symposius and his son and successor Dictinius were Priscillianists, Dictinius having written books in that sense, and both were received back into communion at the first council of Toledo in 400 on renouncing the error, Dictinius's books being condemned while his person was spared. Astorga later gave its name to the Maragato country and stood on the pilgrim road to Compostela. The dictionary records Astorga for the settlement of 400, which is a model of how a church should deal with a bishop who has taught error and recanted: the books condemned, the man received, the office kept, and no blood.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines recantation as the retracting of a declaration; communion as fellowship in the church; restoration as the act of replacing in a former state; abjuration as a renouncing on oath; and lenity as mildness of temper.
webster_full: RECANTATION, n. The act of recanting; a retraction of a declaration or proposition; the declaration that contradicts a former one.
COMMUNION, n. Fellowship; intercourse between two persons or more; mutual participation in the Lord's supper.
RESTORATION, n. The act of replacing in a former state; renewal; re-establishment; recovery.
ABJURATION, n. A renunciation upon oath; the act of renouncing a former opinion or allegiance.
LENITY, n. Mildness of temper; softness; tenderness; mercy in the use of power.
scriptures: Gal 6:1
Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.
In meekness instructing those that oppose themselves; if God peradventure will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth;
Jas 5:19
Brethren, if any of you do err from the truth, and one convert him;
Jas 5:20
Let him know, that he which converteth the sinner from the error of his way shall save a soul from death, and shall hide a multitude of sins.
corruption_summary: Ancient see of Leon whose Priscillianist bishops Symposius and Dictinius were received back at the council of Toledo in 400, their books condemned and their persons spared.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is restoration, which the council of 400 practised and later Spanish church practice abandoned. A bishop who had taught error recanted it and kept his see; his books were condemned by name, which protected the church, and he was not killed, which protected the church too. Paul gives the procedure and attaches a warning to the restorers themselves: “restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted” (Gal 6:1).

The second paragraph names the live temptation, which runs in both directions. One error receives the man and leaves the error standing; the other destroys the man to be rid of the error. Paul's charge holds both together and attaches a hope to the manner: “In meekness instructing those that oppose themselves” (2Ti 2:25). James makes the recovery of a wanderer a saving act and says so in the strongest terms: “if any of you do err from the truth, and one convert him” (Jas 5:19), for “he which converteth the sinner from the error of his way shall save a soul from death” (Jas 5:20). Astorga in 400 did it correctly, and the dictionary says so plainly.

“In meekness instructing those that oppose themselves” (2Ti 2:25) — the manner required of the corrector.
“he which converteth the sinner from the error of his way” (Jas 5:20) — why restoration is worth the trouble.

pos: n. (the Roman capital of Lusitania and metropolitan see of western Spain, scene of the martyrdom of Eulalia under Diocletian)
etymology: From Latin Emerita Augusta, the colony of Augustus's veterans, from emeritus, a discharged soldier.
biblical_def: Merida was founded in 25 before Christ as a settlement for discharged legionaries and became the capital of Roman Lusitania and one of the great cities of the West, with a theatre, amphitheatre, circus and aqueducts still standing. It was a metropolitan see from the fourth century, senior in western Spain until Toledo displaced it, and under the Visigoths its bishops Paul and Fidelis and Masona are known from the Lives of the Fathers of Merida. Its martyr is Eulalia, a girl put to death in the persecution under Diocletian about 304, whose name travelled across Europe in the hymn of Prudentius and in the earliest surviving text in French. The city fell to the Muslims in 713 and never recovered its rank. The dictionary records Merida for Eulalia, and for the plain fact she represents: the faith was planted in Spain by the testimony of people with no power at all, three centuries before any Spanish king was Christian and twelve before any Spanish king was a persecutor.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a martyr as one who suffers death for his religion; a colony as a body of people settled in a distant land; a metropolitan as the bishop of a mother church; testimony as a solemn declaration; and constancy as firmness of mind.
webster_full: MARTYR, n. One who suffers death in defense of the christian faith, or in defense of any cause which he believes to be just.
COLONY, n. A company of people transplanted from their mother country to a remote province or country, and remaining subject to the jurisdiction of the parent state.
METROPOLITAN, n. A bishop who presides over the other bishops of a province; an archbishop.
TESTIMONY, n. A solemn declaration or affirmation made for the purpose of establishing or proving some fact.
CONSTANCY, n. Fixedness; firmness of mind; steadiness; perseverance in a purpose or opinion.
scriptures: And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death.
Act 1:8

But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.
But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;
Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven.
corruption_summary: Roman capital of Lusitania and early metropolitan see, scene of the martyrdom of Eulalia under Diocletian about 304.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the gospel came to Spain from below. Eulalia was a girl with no rank in a garrison town, and her death was recorded, hymned and remembered across Europe for fifteen centuries. Paul states the pattern as deliberate on God's part rather than accidental: “But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty” (1Co 1:27).

The second paragraph names the live temptation, which is to assume that Christianity advances by holding institutions. In Spain it arrived as testimony under sentence and later held every institution in the country, and the second condition did it less good than the first. The commission is a promise of witnesses rather than of magistrates, “and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria” (Act 1:8); the overcoming is by testimony and blood, “they loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11); and the thing required of the obscure believer is simply to own Christ aloud: “Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven” (Mat 10:32).

Greek asthenes (G0772) — weak, feeble, without strength; “God hath chosen the weak things of the world”, 1 Corinthians 1:27.
Greek kataischuno (G2617) — to put to shame, to confound; “to confound the things which are mighty”, 1 Corinthians 1:27.
Greek homologeo (G3670) — to confess, to acknowledge openly; “Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men”, Matthew 10:32.
Greek agapao (G0025) — to love; “they loved not their lives unto the death”, Revelation 12:11.

“ye shall be witnesses unto me” (Act 1:8) — a promise of witnesses, not of magistrates.
“Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men” (Mat 10:32) — what was asked of a girl in a garrison town.

pos: n. (the capital of Navarre, annexed by Castile in 1512, at whose siege in 1521 Ignatius Loyola was wounded and turned to religion)
etymology: From Latin Pompaelo, the town of Pompey, who founded it about 75 before Christ.
biblical_def: Pamplona is the capital of Navarre, a Basque city founded by Pompey, the seat of its kings and its bishops, and the place where Navarre's independence ended when Ferdinand annexed the kingdom south of the Pyrenees in 1512. On the twentieth of May 1521, during a French attempt to recover the city, a Basque gentleman of the garrison named Inigo Lopez de Loyola had his leg broken by a cannon ball; convalescing at Loyola with nothing to read but a life of Christ and a book of saints' lives, he resolved on a religious career, and from that resolution came the Spiritual Exercises and in 1540 the Society of Jesus. The dictionary records Pamplona as the place where the most effective opponent the Reformation ever had was made, and records the manner of it carefully. Loyola was converted by two books in a sickroom because there was nothing else at hand. What a man finds on the shelf when he is finally made still is not a small matter.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a siege as the sitting down of an army before a place; convalescence as a gradual recovery of health; an exercise as a putting into practice; a society as an association of persons; and a vocation as a calling or employment.
webster_full: SIEGE, n. The setting of an army around or before a fortified place for the purpose of compelling the garrison to surrender.
CONVALESCENCE, n. Renewal of health; the insensible recovery of health and strength after disease.
EXERCISE, n. In theology, the performance of the duties of religion; practice; use; employment.
SOCIETY, n. The union of a number of rational beings; a number of persons united, either for a temporary or permanent object.
VOCATION, n. A calling by the will of God; a summons; a call to the knowledge and enjoyment of the gospel; employment; business.
scriptures: The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?
corruption_summary: Capital of Navarre, annexed by Castile in 1512, where the wounding of Ignatius Loyola at the siege of 1521 began the chain that produced the Society of Jesus.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the substitution of devotional literature for the Scriptures, which is the very thing that happened in that sickroom and which the dictionary does not pretend was unimportant. A man with a broken leg and a serious soul was handed a harmonised life of Christ and a legendary of the saints; what he built from them was a religion of method, obedience and imitation, enormously effective and resting on a shelf of the wrong books. The text itself claims the office those books took: “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is the sufficiency and the priority of Scripture in forming a soul. Paul credits Timothy's whole formation to early acquaintance with it, “from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures” (2Ti 3:15); Luke commends the hearers who checked even an apostle against it, who “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11); and Jeremiah describes the effect of the word in terms no life of a saint can imitate: “Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?” (Jer 23:29). The dictionary names Pamplona as an argument for putting Bibles where sick men can reach them.

Hebrew pethi (H6612) — simple, untaught; “it giveth understanding unto the simple”, Psalm 119:130.
Greek graphe (G1124) — a writing, the Scriptures; “from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures”, 2 Timothy 3:15.
Greek anakrino (G0350) — to examine, to sift; “and searched the scriptures daily”, Acts 17:11.

usage: “The entrance of thy words giveth light” (Psa 119:130) — the office those two books took.
“from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures” (2Ti 3:15) — the formation Loyola did not have.
“and searched the scriptures daily” (Act 17:11) — the habit that would have changed the outcome.

pos: n. (the Aragonese see and university town, the Roman Osca where Sertorius founded a school for the sons of Spanish chiefs)
etymology: From Latin Osca, an Iberian town of the Ilergetes, of pre-Roman origin.
biblical_def: Huesca lies in the Aragonese foothills of the Pyrenees. As Roman Osca it was the base of Sertorius, the rebel governor who about 77 before Christ founded there a school to teach the sons of Spanish chieftains Latin and Greek, a device for binding a province by educating its heirs. Huesca was recovered from Muslim rule in 1096, became the Aragonese capital for a time, and received a university charter in 1354, one of the oldest in Spain. The dictionary records Huesca because the Sertorian school is the clearest ancient instance of a policy that every religious and political power since has used: take the children, teach them your language and your loyalties, and the next generation needs no conquering. The Jesuits used it, the Reformed used it in Geneva and Scotland, and modern states use it. The dictionary therefore says what it believes about the method: it works, it is lawful, and the question is never whether children will be formed but who forms them and with what.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a school as a place for instruction; a hostage as a person delivered as security; loyalty as faithfulness to a prince or lawful government; language as human speech; and nurture as that which nourishes or trains.
webster_full: SCHOOL, n. A place or house in which persons are instructed in arts, science, languages or any species of learning.
HOSTAGE, n. A person delivered to an enemy as a pledge for the performance of the conditions of a treaty.
LOYALTY, n. Fidelity to a prince or sovereign, or to a husband or lover; faithfulness to lawful government.
LANGUAGE, n. Human speech; the expression of ideas by words or significant articulate sounds, for the communication of thoughts.
NURTURE, n. That which nourishes; food; diet; education; instruction; the act of bringing up.
scriptures: Deu 6:7
And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
Eph 6:4
And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.
Dan 1:4

Children in whom was no blemish, but well favoured, and skilful in all wisdom, and cunning in knowledge, and understanding science, and such as had ability in them to stand in the king's palace, and whom they might teach the learning and the tongue of the Chaldeans.
Dan 1:8

But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the portion of the king's meat, nor with the wine which he drank: therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself.
corruption_summary: Aragonese see and university town, the Roman Osca where Sertorius founded a school to form the sons of Spanish chiefs in Latin and Greek.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the formation of children is a contested field and always has been. Babylon ran the Sertorian policy before Sertorius, selecting Hebrew youths who were “Children in whom was no blemish, but well favoured, and skilful in all wisdom” (Dan 1:4) and teaching them the learning and the tongue of the Chaldeans. The policy was intelligent and it largely failed with Daniel, for a stated reason: “But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself” (Dan 1:8).

The second paragraph names the live temptation, which is for Christian parents to assume that formation is what happens at school rather than what happens at home. Scripture puts the weight on the household and makes it continual rather than scheduled, “And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children” (Deu 6:7), and it addresses fathers specifically with the content as well as the duty: bring them up “in the nurture and admonition of the Lord” (Eph 6:4). Daniel learned Chaldean and refused the king's table. The dictionary holds that a child so formed can be educated anywhere, and a child not so formed will be formed by whoever has him.

Hebrew mum (H3971) — a blemish, a defect; “Children in whom was no blemish”, Daniel 1:4.
Hebrew sim (H7760) — to set, to place, to purpose; “But Daniel purposed in his heart”, Daniel 1:8.
Hebrew ga'al (H1351) — to defile, to pollute; “that he would not defile himself”, Daniel 1:8.

“But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself” (Dan 1:8) — why it failed with him.
“And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children” (Deu 6:7) — where the weight actually lies.

pos: n. (the Aragonese capital of the 380 council against the Priscillianists and of the 1485 murder of the inquisitor Pedro de Arbues)
etymology: From Latin Caesaraugusta, the city of Caesar Augustus, through Arabic Saraqusta.
biblical_def: Saragossa is the capital of Aragon, on the Ebro, founded as Caesaraugusta by Augustus and a Christian centre from the third century, with its own martyrs under Diocletian. The council of Saragossa in 380 issued the first canons against the Priscillianists, dealing with private assemblies, fasting on Sundays, the reading of Scripture in houses and the absence of the faithful from church in Lent; it is the earliest Western legislation of its kind and it reads as a church trying to manage a lay movement of Bible-reading ascetics. In 1485 the inquisitor Pedro de Arbues was stabbed in the cathedral by conversos, which ended Aragonese resistance to the royal tribunal. The dictionary records Saragossa because the 380 canons mark a decision whose consequences ran for a thousand years: the church answered an irregular enthusiasm for Scripture and fasting by restricting private meetings rather than by teaching better, and it has repeated that mistake in every generation since.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a canon as a law of the church; a conventicle as a private assembly for worship; asceticism is not in Webster, but to fast is to abstain from food; enthusiasm as a heated imagination in religion; and regulation as the act of reducing to order.
webster_full: CANON, n. In church affairs, a law or rule of doctrine or discipline, enacted by a council and confirmed by authority.
CONVENTICLE, n. An assembly or gathering; appropriately, an assembly for religious worship, in contempt, as of dissenters.
FAST, v.i. To abstain from food, beyond the usual time; to abstain from food voluntarily, for the mortification of the body.
ENTHUSIASM, n. A belief or conceit of private revelation; heat of imagination; elevation of fancy in religion.
REGULATION, n. The act of regulating or reducing to order; a rule or order prescribed by authority.
scriptures: Act 2:46
And they, continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart,
And how I kept back nothing that was profitable unto you, but have shewed you, and have taught you publickly, and from house to house,
Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
corruption_summary: Aragonese capital of the council of 380 whose canons restricted private Scripture meetings against the Priscillianists, and of the 1485 murder of Pedro de Arbues.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the suppression of household religion as a disciplinary tactic. The Priscillianists had real errors, and the canons of 380 did not chiefly address those errors; they addressed meetings in houses, reading the Scriptures outside the church building, and private fasts. That answer leaves the error standing and removes the practice the New Testament commends, since the first Christians met in both places: they continued “daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house” (Act 2:46).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. Paul describes his own ministry as public and domestic together, having taught “publickly, and from house to house” (Act 20:20), so a church that forbids the second half is not protecting the first. The right instrument against error is examination, not prohibition: “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good” (1Th 5:21), and the Bereans are commended for the very habit the Saragossan canons curtailed, since they “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11). The dictionary concludes that the answer to a bad Bible study is a better one.
